clue.text: Brit not quite overcome by a task all too tricky for Li Na?

indicators.note: the trimmed word is overcome, surrounded, by the rearranged letters that follow
something too tricky to sort out is jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a limey is American slang for a British person

explanation.surface: A British player is beaten by the Chinese tennis star Li Na in a hard-fought match.
explanation.walkthrough: Li Na looks like the tennis champion, but read as chemical symbols it is lithium and sodium. A limey is American slang for a Brit; 'not quite' drops its last letter, and 'overcome by' sets the rest inside the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithium (Li) and sodium (Na) are both members of group 1 of the periodic table, the reactive family that gives this name.

clue.text: He came, he saw, he conquered … but he never appeared to do this

definitions.text: He came, he saw, he conquered … but he never appeared to do this

parts.words: He came, he saw, he conquered … but he never appeared to do this
parts.note: Caesar's boast lists three deeds, like three acts of a play; there was no fourth deed, and in Shakespeare's play he is killed in the third act

explanation.surface: Julius Caesar's famous boast of three achievements, with a hint that something was missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The three verbs read as three acts, so the missing next one is the fourth; Shakespeare's Caesar is also dead by then, returning only as a ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar is assassinated in Act III, so the living Caesar takes no part in the following section of the drama.

clue.text: Time mum's out of tie and raincoat (mock fashion)!

indicators.note: says the letters for time and mum leave the words for tie and raincoat

parts.note: a knot is a tie in a rope or cord
a mackintosh is a waterproof coat
Ma is a familiar word for mother
to ape is to mimic or mock

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a fashion statement made from a tie and a raincoat, with Mum no longer in charge of dressing them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' takes T and MA from the joined tie and raincoat words. 'Fashion' is a verb here, not the clothing trade the surface suggests, and 'mock' is a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion something is to shape or form it, which is what this idiom means: to mould into proper form.

clue.text: Comparatively little: what's charged to enter zoo's attraction

indicators.note: says the charged particle goes into the word for comparatively little

parts.note: less is the comparative of little
an ion is an electrically charged particle

explanation.surface: A cheap admission fee charged to get into a zoo, a modest attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's charged' looks like an entry fee but is the physics particle.
explanation.definitionFit: A female big cat is the kind of animal visitors flock to see at a zoo, so it is a zoo's draw.

clue.text: See 1
Moderate English: one contractor's location for Nice

parts.note: a means one
someone who contracts words would write the city's position as SE of F, south-east of France

explanation.surface: An English builder working in Nice is asked to tone things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contractor' is not a builder but someone who abbreviates: Nice lies in the south-east of France, shortened to SE of F.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate is to lessen in intensity, which is what the phrasal verb means: to slacken or relax.

clue.text: Film notice written by pundits about that year's output?

indicators.note: the notice and pundits words go about, around, the rearranged letters

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement, a notice
aces are experts, the sort of people who act as pundits

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are turned out in a new arrangement, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive 's is not counted, leaving the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A film review written by critics assessing the whole year's releases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pundits' suggests TV commentators, but aces are experts. 'Written by' just sets the notice beside them, and the pair go 'about' the jumbled letters. The film is the 1937 Marx Brothers comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of a Marx Brothers comedy feature from 1937, set around a racecourse and a sanatorium.

clue.text: Slowhand initially right to enter fifth band for cover

indicators.note: says the initials and the letter for right go into the word for band

parts.note: a set is a group of musicians' performance, or a band of people
Slowhand is the nickname of guitarist Eric Clapton, whose initials are EC
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Eric Clapton joins a fifth group to play a cover version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' looks like a cover version of a song, but it means to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceal or hide something away is to keep it covered, a sense of the verb meaning to stash out of sight.

clue.text: Don't protest so much about a striking demo

parts.note: to ... is to protest, so protesting less is to ... less
on means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Protesters are told to tone it down at a demo where workers are striking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demo' and 'striking' suggest an industrial protest; here a demo is a demonstration, a practical example, and striking means memorable.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a vivid practical illustration that teaches a principle, which is a memorable demonstration.

clue.text: "Terrible" Ivan's rock bottom as an old statesman!

indicators.note: Ivan the Terrible gives the word, which here says the following letters are wrecked and rearranged

parts.note: the possessive is taken as the letters of the name with S
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ivan the Terrible hits rock bottom as a statesman of old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' looks like Ivan's famous epithet, but it is the anagram signal; the apostrophe S here supplies an S letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Chancellor unified Germany in 1871 and was a dominant nineteenth-century European politician.

clue.text: Regularly tough person showing PC ID

definitions.meaning: a person regularly described as tough
a small file a website stores on a computer to identify it

explanation.surface: A hard-nosed official checking a police constable's identity papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' suggests taking alternate letters, but it means the word usually comes after tough; PC suggests a police constable but means a personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A resilient individual is called a tough one of these, and a browser stores small tracking files with the same name.

clue.text: Green flag slippery customer's locked in business and research centre

indicators.note: the slippery creature has the others shut inside it, so its letters go round them

parts.note: an eel is the proverbial slippery customer, and the 's stands for has
CO is the abbreviation for company, a business
a lab is a laboratory, a centre for research

explanation.surface: A green signal shows that a crook has been locked up inside a company's research facility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green flag' looks like a go signal, but it is an environmental label.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a mark on a product signalling environmental credentials, so a sign flagging something as eco-friendly.

clue.text: Toy restaurant's covered in itself

indicators.note: the restaurant word covers, encloses, the Latin phrase

parts.note: trat is a short form of trattoria, an Italian restaurant
in se is Latin for in itself

explanation.surface: A toy restaurant smothered in its own food.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAT is short for trattoria, and IN SE is the Latin phrase for 'in itself'; 'covered' means the first goes round the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's model railway with track and engines is a classic plaything sold as a boxed kit.

clue.text: See 2
Assemblyman's in better health

definitions.meaning: a worker who puts together machine parts, a mechanic
comparative of the adjective meaning healthy

explanation.surface: A member of a legislature is in better shape than before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assemblyman' suggests a politician but means a man who assembles things.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanic who puts parts together has this job title, and the comparative of an adjective for healthy is spelt the same.

clue.text: It's for notes and it's back in pocket

indicators.note: says the turned letters go inside the word for pocket

parts.note: the pot is the kitty, or a pool of money one pockets

indicators.note: says the letters of it's are read from end to start

parts.note: taken as the letters I, T, S

explanation.surface: A note-holder kept in a pocket and taken back out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns ITS into STI, which goes 'in' POT; pot also means to pocket a ball in snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the brand name for small sticky slips of paper on which reminders are jotted.

clue.text: Keep an eye on bishop's position, ever so precarious on king's file

definitions.text: Keep an eye on bishop's position

indicators.note: something precarious is unstable, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
in chess the king starts on the e-file, so the letter E

explanation.surface: A chess player watches a bishop left exposed on the king's file.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Precarious' rearranges EVER SO to OVERSE. The definition is extended: the word bishop comes from Greek episkopos, an overseer, so supervising is a bishop's role.
explanation.definitionFit: To supervise or watch over is the duty of a bishop, whose title derives from the Greek for overseer.

clue.text: A weight lifted off uncovered bunk

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting a word turns it upside down, so it reads bottom to top
with its covering stripped away, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: food that is off is addled, gone rotten

explanation.surface: A weightlifter drops a weight onto an unmade bunk bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' turns A WT into TWA; 'uncovered' strips ADDLED to DDLE. 'Bunk' looks like a bed but means nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunk is short for bunkum, meaning nonsense or silly talk, a synonym of this word.

clue.text: Can I take a butcher's consideration?

definitions.meaning: butcher's hook is Cockney rhyming slang for look, so asking to have a look
what someone says while pondering a question

explanation.surface: A customer asks the butcher whether they may take some meat, as a matter of thought.
explanation.walkthrough: A butcher's is British rhyming slang: butcher's hook rhymes with look, so taking a butcher's is having a look.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a request to look at something and a filler said while thinking something over.

clue.text: See 8
Reverse sides of glass cart

indicators.note: sides here are left and right, L and R, so those two letters swap places

parts.note: a tumbler is a drinking glass

explanation.surface: An instruction to turn a glass around on a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sides' are L (left) and R (right): swapping them in TUMBLER turns LER into REL.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbril is a farm cart, famously the one carrying condemned prisoners to the guillotine in the French Revolution.

clue.text: No sense being like this in Gaza

definitions.text: No sense being like this in Gaza

parts.words: No sense being like this in Gaza
parts.note: Milton's Samson Agonistes describes the blinded Samson as sightless in Gaza, a phrase Huxley used as a title

explanation.surface: A remark that there is no point being in this state in Gaza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No sense' reads as 'pointless' but means lacking the sense of sight; the phrase comes from Milton and Huxley.
explanation.definitionFit: Samson, blinded by the Philistines, is described by Milton as without sight in Gaza; lacking vision is lacking a sense.

clue.text: Notices the crewmen are dazed

parts.note: sees means notices
tars are sailors, members of a ship's crew

explanation.surface: Someone notices that the ship's crew are in a daze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' looks like a noun, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: After a blow to the head people are said to perceive twinkling lights, an idiom for being stunned.

clue.text: Clear sign evident, indicating this animal's back …

indicators.note: says the joined words are read in reverse

parts.note: to net is to clear as profit
the Ram, Aries, is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: An obvious mark shows that this animal has returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns NET and RAM into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a weasel-like woodland mammal, the animal the clue points to.

clue.text: See 6
… and it's me that's in the wrong!

parts.note: the letters I STAND, once corrected (rearranged), give the clue words and it's

explanation.surface: Someone admits a mistake, continuing from the clue before.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay, with 'corrected' rearranging I STAND, and it gives 'and it's'. The ellipsis ties it to the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom is a formal admission of error, accepting that someone else has put one right.

clue.text: Morning refreshers taking care of quite a lot of publicity tests

indicators.note: one thing takes care of another by holding it, so the snack word goes round the shortened publicity word

parts.note: elevenses is a British mid-morning snack or tea break

indicators.note: most of the word but not all, so its last letter goes

parts.note: a plug is a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: Morning tea breaks are used to look after much of the publicity for some exams.
explanation.walkthrough: ELEVENSES is a British mid-morning break for tea and biscuits. 'Quite a lot of' trims PLUG to PLU.
explanation.definitionFit: These were the selection exams English pupils sat at about age eleven to decide grammar school places.

clue.text: See 25
